profile.summary: The evaluation from the BERTax paper: assign 1,500 nt genome fragments to superkingdom, phylum and, in one dataset, genus. BERTax is compared with Kraken2, sourmash, MMseqs2, minimap2 and DeepMicrobes, all given the same reference or training data, on a closely related split and a genus-held-out split. It is for people choosing a taxonomic classifier, especially for sequences without close relatives in reference databases.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Comparison to Other Classification Approaches

summary_quotes.text: Here we present BERTax, a deep neural network program based on natural language processing to precisely classify the superkingdom and phylum of DNA sequences taxonomically without the need for a known representative relative from a database.
For each superkingdom, we extracted 1 million fragments of length 1,500 nt from the downloaded genomes at uniformly distributed starting positions.

It has to be noted that all methods compared against have exactly the same reference or training data available as BERTax, to allow for a meaningful comparison. For approaches that normally include whole genomes in their reference data, this presents a necessary deviation from the designed use case for these methods.

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: How well a method assigns the taxonomic origin of a DNA fragment when close relatives are, or are not, in the reference data. The distantly related dataset simulates unknown sequences by holding out whole genera.

quotes.text: Here we present BERTax, a deep neural network program based on natural language processing to precisely classify the superkingdom and phylum of DNA sequences taxonomically without the need for a known representative relative from a database.
For this purpose, a genus separation between training and test sets is employed; that is, for no sample in the test set does there exist a sample of the same genus in the training set

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Genomes of archaea, eukaryotes, bacteria and viruses were taken from NCBI, and 1 million 1,500 nt fragments per superkingdom were extracted, then clustered at 80% identity. Fine-tuning data keep phyla with at least 10,000 fragments: 30 phylum classes and 2,328,584 samples. The closely related dataset tests on 2,000 random samples per phylum; the distantly related dataset tests on whole held-out genera, balanced to 1,780 samples per phylum; the final model dataset adds 2 million eukaryotic and bacterial fragments and has 5 superkingdom, 44 phylum and 156 genus classes, split like the closely related dataset. In every case 95% of the rest is training and 5% validation.

quotes.text: Archaean and eukaryotic genomes were retrieved from NCBI using ncbi-genome-download
viral and bacterial genomes were downloaded from NCBI manually.
For each superkingdom, we extracted 1 million fragments of length 1,500 nt from the downloaded genomes at uniformly distributed starting positions.
we clustered fragments by sequence identity using MMseqs2-linclust version 11.e1a1c
This results in 30 phylum classes with 2,328,584 samples in total.

The first evaluation dataset is called the closely related dataset. As a test set, we randomly select 2,000 samples per phylum. From the remaining samples, we select 95% of the samples of each phylum as the training set and use the remaining 5% as the validation set
For this purpose, a genus separation between training and test sets is employed; that is, for no sample in the test set does there exist a sample of the same genus in the training set
We keep 1,780 samples per phylum (according to the smallest subset).

With this, the number of classes per taxonomic rank is five for the rank superkingdom, 44 for phylum, and 156 for genera. We partition this dataset into training, validation, and test sets using closely related selection as described above
We selected only classes with at least 10,000 fragments.

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Each tool is scored by macro average precision (AveP) at superkingdom and phylum, and at genus for the final dataset. Database tools get only the training partition as reference, default parameters are used, and MMseqs2 is also run with taxonomy parameters to obtain a confidence for precision-recall curves. DeepMicrobes is trained on the same data. The share of sequences each tool classifies is reported alongside, since database tools leave some unclassified.

quotes.text: Comparison of the macro AveP on all three datasets
Taxonomic classification ranks considered are superkingdom (Supk.), phylum (Phyl.), or genus (only final selection dataset).

It has to be noted that all methods compared against have exactly the same reference or training data available as BERTax, to allow for a meaningful comparison. For approaches that normally include whole genomes in their reference data, this presents a necessary deviation from the designed use case for these methods.
For all tools, we used the default parameters.
The DeepMicrobes models are trained on exactly the same data as BERTax.

The proportion of classified sequences varies between 6.90% for sourmash and 92.69% for MMseqs2 taxonomy*. Neural network approaches like BERTax and DeepMicrobes always reach 100% due to their mode of operation without confidence thresholds.

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Macro average precision (AveP); higher is better. Proportion of sequences classified is also reported.

quotes.text: In raw numbers (macro average precision [AveP]), the performance improvement gained with BERTax is most visible for sequences from unknown genera, where an increase from 76.91 to 87.57% on the level of superkingdoms and from 50.51 to 60.34% on the phylum level can be achieved, compared with DeepMicrobes, both in combination with MMseqs2.
Comparison of the macro AveP on all three datasets

The proportion of classified sequences varies between 6.90% for sourmash and 92.69% for MMseqs2 taxonomy*. Neural network approaches like BERTax and DeepMicrobes always reach 100% due to their mode of operation without confidence thresholds.

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Kraken2, sourmash, MMseqs2 (and MMseqs2 taxonomy*), minimap2 and DeepMicrobes; combinations of MMseqs2 with BERTax or DeepMicrobes.

quotes.text: BERTax is compared against the state-of-the-art database taxonomic classification approaches Kraken2
As a state-of-the-art machine learning approach, we tested DeepMicrobes
Using this strategy, MMseqs2 + BERTax (99.33% and 94.84%) performs better than MMseqs2 + DeepMicrobes (99.33% and 93.67%).

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Duplicate samples between training and test are not allowed, and the distantly related set holds out whole genera. Homologous sequences between training and test were deliberately kept.
